understanding.purpose: An order-fulfillment table listing items, quantities, charges, warehouse locations, and shipment tracking.
understanding.reading: Readers scan each row as one item, compare quantities and charges down their columns, and follow the row across to find its warehouse and tracking identifier.
groups: ID and SKU identify the item; Color and Size describe the variant.
Qty, Price, Tax, and Total form the numeric order and cost group.
Warehouse and Tracking describe fulfillment and shipment.
keep_intact: Tracking identifiers and dashes indicating no tracking.
Color and size values, column headers, and warehouse location codes where possible.
may_wrap: SKU codes at natural hyphen breaks.
Warehouse location codes at natural hyphen breaks, while keeping the Warehouse header intact.

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Keep r2C's natural SKU and warehouse wraps, but give Tracking its full 180px. The table is 759px wide, requiring 40px of horizontal scrolling while preserving every tracking identifier.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Give SKU more room to test a more legible two-line arrangement while keeping the warehouse and tracking treatment from r0A. The 774px table trades a little more scrolling for less fragmented item identifiers.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Keep SKUs on one line as in r0C, but allow warehouse codes to wrap at hyphens. This reduces the table to 821px while preserving intact tracking identifiers and potentially shortening the scroll.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Widen Warehouse enough for its longest full location while retaining naturally wrapped SKUs. This tests whether single-line locations improve row scanning enough to justify 80px of horizontal overflow.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Give both SKU and Warehouse their full one-line widths. This should produce compact single-line rows and intact values, at the cost of 142px of horizontal overflow.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Preserve complete tracking identifiers and allow warehouse codes to wrap, while giving SKU 20px more room to test whether its line breaks and visual rhythm improve. The resulting table is 779px wide, with 60px of overflow.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: Fit the table within 719px by narrowing Tracking. This tests the no-scroll alternative, accepting mid-identifier splits and potentially taller rows.
bad.why: Tracking identifiers split across lines inside the codes, making them harder to scan and transcribe.

bad.name: r3B
bad.note: Give Tracking 140px of text space, reducing overflow to 21px. This tests whether a small scroll and a shorter tracking split provide a useful compromise when keeping the whole identifier intact is less important than keeping most of the table visible.
bad.why: Tracking identifiers still split inside the codes, while the table also requires horizontal scrolling.

rationale: r3A preserves complete tracking identifiers and keeps the full header visible, with only 39px beyond the viewport. SKU and warehouse values wrap at hyphens, so each row remains legible without widening the table substantially. The wider designs make some values easier to scan, but place more of the tracking column beyond the initial view.

general: Protect identifiers from arbitrary breaks when readers may need to compare or transcribe them.
Allocate width according to content and scanning needs; related numeric columns can remain compact while longer text receives more space.
Judge horizontal overflow together with what remains visible at first sight and the readability gained by scrolling.
specific: SKU and warehouse values can wrap at hyphens, whereas tracking values have no natural break points.
All three data rows are already two lines tall in r3A, so modest extra width in one wrapped column alone does not shorten the table.

tradeoffs: r2B keeps every value on one line and makes rows easier to scan, but requires 142px of scrolling and leaves much of Tracking outside the initial viewport. r2C fits the viewport but splits tracking codes.
uncertain: A designer prioritizing frequent SKU or warehouse comparisons could reasonably prefer r1C or r2A. The ranges are approximate individual adjustments around r3A; simultaneous increases would add overflow and may change the balance.

critique.good: Headers, numeric values and tracking identifiers stay intact. The complete table is almost visible within the viewport, and warehouse codes wrap at hyphens.
critique.problems: Each SKU occupies four lines, making the rows unusually tall and leaving large empty areas across the numeric columns. The fragmented SKU is also harder to recognize as one identifier. The final edge of tracking sits just beyond the viewport.
critique.cause: The 65px SKU column provides only 44px for text, forcing several hyphen breaks. The 102px Warehouse column causes a shorter, two-line wrap. The 180px Tracking column preserves the identifiers but contributes to the 9px overflow.

critique.good: Headers and numeric values remain intact, warehouse codes break at hyphens, and almost the entire table fits within the viewport.
critique.problems: The SKU column still produces four-line rows and considerable empty space. Both tracking identifiers split before their final digit, making them harder to read and verify.
critique.cause: The 65px SKU width fragments the item codes. Reducing Tracking to 172px leaves only 151px of text space, less than the 159px identifier width.

critique.good: Every value stays on one line, giving the table compact rows and making SKU, warehouse and tracking identifiers easy to read. The numeric group has a clear, consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: Tracking lies largely beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to see shipment identifiers. The extra width also separates fulfillment information from the item details at first sight.
critique.cause: The 157px SKU and 143px Warehouse columns accommodate their longest values on one line; together with the 180px Tracking column, they make the table 142px wider than the viewport.

critique.good: The compact layout keeps the numeric columns easy to compare and all headers and tracking identifiers intact. SKU and warehouse values wrap at hyphens, giving the rows a consistent two-line rhythm.
critique.problems: The first view cuts through the tracking identifiers, so readers must scroll to see their ends. The warehouse wraps in every row, making the table taller.
critique.cause: Tracking needs its full 180px, but the table totals 759px. The 102px warehouse column keeps its header intact but leaves too little text width for the full location codes.

critique.good: The headers and numeric values remain intact, and the item and fulfillment codes wrap at natural breaks.
critique.problems: The extra SKU width does not visibly reduce wrapping or row height. It moves more of the tracking column beyond the viewport without a compensating benefit.
critique.cause: Increasing SKU from 95px to 110px is still insufficient for the full SKU values, while increasing total width to 774px.

critique.good: Full SKUs are easy to scan and compare, while the numeric columns and headers remain intact.
critique.problems: The unwrapped SKUs do not shorten the rows because warehouse locations still wrap. Tracking begins close to the viewport edge, leaving most of each identifier to be reached by scrolling.
critique.cause: The 157px SKU column removes SKU wraps, but the 102px warehouse column still forces two-line rows. Together with the 180px tracking column, the table reaches 821px.

critique.good: All headers, amounts, warehouse codes and tracking identifiers stay intact. The SKU wraps at hyphens, and the two-line rows give the table a consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: The tracking identifiers extend beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to see their ends. The full-width warehouse column uses space that could bring more of tracking into view.
critique.cause: The 180px Tracking column preserves the 159px identifiers, but the 143px Warehouse column keeps locations on one line and contributes to the 80px overflow.

critique.good: Every value fits on one line, producing compact rows that are easy to compare vertically. Identifiers and location codes remain intact.
critique.problems: The wide table puts much of Tracking beyond the initial viewport, separating shipment details from the rest of each row until the reader scrolls.
critique.cause: The 157px SKU and 143px Warehouse columns prevent wrapping but make the table 862px wide, with 142px beyond the viewport.

critique.good: The entire table fits initially. Headers and numeric values remain intact, and SKU and warehouse codes wrap at natural hyphens. The consistent two-line rows support scanning across.
critique.problems: The two tracking identifiers split within their character sequences, making them harder to read and copy accurately. The empty second line in the third Tracking cell also makes the wrapping feel uneven.
critique.cause: Tracking has only 119px of text space at 140px total width, less than the 159px needed for the identifiers. Warehouse at 102px causes its codes to wrap, which is an acceptable trade for recovering space.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r2C.why: The table fits the viewport, and the numeric columns scan clearly. SKU and warehouse values wrap at hyphens, but tracking identifiers split across lines.

r1B.why: SKU and warehouse values wrap reasonably, but the tracking identifiers extend beyond their column and the viewport, making the table boundary misleading.

ref_equal.why: Warehouse and Tracking headers split within words, while SKU, warehouse and tracking values fragment over several lines. Wide short-value columns leave little room for the identifiers.

ref_auto.why: Tracking identifiers remain intact and the table fits the viewport. The narrow SKU column forces each identifier onto four lines, creating tall rows.

r3A.why: The compact SKU and warehouse wrapping supports scanning, but tracking identifiers overflow their column and extend beyond the viewport.

r1C.why: SKU and tracking identifiers remain intact, with clear numeric columns and moderate warehouse wrapping. Tracking sits partly beyond the initial viewport and requires horizontal scrolling.

raw.unsure: The images suggest B and E allow tracking text to overflow its cell; the exact extent of the overflow is difficult to judge at the image edge. F's advantage depends on accepting horizontal scrolling to keep identifiers intact.

ref_equal.why: Equal-looking columns leave excess space in short fields while SKU, warehouse names, tracking values, and even headers break across multiple lines. The tall rows are hard to scan.

r1B.why: Most columns scan well, but the tracking values run beyond the viewport and appear to overflow their allocated column. SKU and warehouse values wrap into two lines.

r2C.why: The compact fields are proportioned well, and SKU and warehouse values wrap at hyphens. Tracking values split across two lines, but the whole table fits in the viewport.

r3A.why: The short fields and two-line SKU and warehouse values are readable, but tracking values extend beyond the viewport and appear to overflow their column.

r1C.why: SKU values remain intact and the numeric columns scan cleanly. Tracking lies partly beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to see the full identifiers.

ref_auto.why: Tracking values remain intact and the full table fits in the viewport, but the narrow SKU column breaks each identifier into four lines, making rows unnecessarily tall and SKUs harder to compare.

raw.unsure: The screenshots make it difficult to distinguish column overflow from the portion of the table reached by horizontal scrolling in B, D, and E. The choice between C and F also depends on whether intact tracking values matter more than readily scanned SKUs.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
